# Job Chapter 34 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 429r–429v

---

**1** Elihu continued: **2** "Listen to me, you wise men! Pay attention, all of you who think you understand. **3** The ear tests words the way the tongue tastes food.

**4** Let us decide together what is right; let us determine among ourselves what is good. **5** Job has said, 'I am innocent, but God has denied me justice. **6** Even though I am right, I am considered a liar. My wound is beyond healing, though I have not sinned.'

**7** Has there ever been anyone like Job? He gulps down mockery like water! **8** He keeps company with evildoers and walks alongside the wicked. **9** For he has declared, 'There is no profit in trying to please God.'

**10** So listen to me, you men of sense — it is unthinkable that God would do evil, or that the Almighty would pervert justice! **11** He pays people back for what they have done and gives them what their conduct deserves. **12** It is absolutely true: God does not do wrong. The Almighty never twists justice.

**13** Who put him in charge of the earth? Who appointed him over the whole world? **14** If God decided to withdraw his spirit and breath, **15** every living thing would die at once, and humanity would return to dust.

**16** Now if you have any understanding, listen to this: **17** Could someone who hates justice actually govern? Will you condemn the Righteous One, the Mighty One? **18** He is the one who says to kings, 'You are worthless!' and to nobles, 'You are wicked!' **19** He shows no favoritism to rulers and does not prefer the rich over the poor, because he made them all.

**20** People die in an instant, in the middle of the night. The mighty are swept away — and not by any human hand. **21** For God's eyes are on everything people do; he watches every step they take. **22** There is no darkness deep enough, no shadow dark enough, to hide evildoers from him.

**23** God does not need to examine people any further before bringing them to judgment. **24** He shatters the powerful without even conducting an inquiry, and puts others in their place. **25** Because he knows what they have done, he overturns them overnight and they are destroyed. **26** He strikes them down for their wickedness where everyone can see, **27** because they turned away from following him and completely ignored his ways, **28** and they caused the cry of the poor and the oppressed to reach his ears.

**29** But when God remains silent, who has the right to condemn him? When he hides his face, who can find him? Yet he watches over nations and individuals alike, **30** preventing the godless from ruling and keeping the people from being trapped.

**31** Suppose someone says to God, 'I have suffered enough; I will not sin again. **32** Show me what I cannot see; if I have done wrong, I will stop.'

**33** Should God then reward you on your terms, just because you disagree? You are the one who must choose, not me — so tell us what you think.

**34** People with good sense will tell me — any wise person listening will agree: **35** 'Job speaks without knowledge; there is no insight in his words.' **36** If only Job could be tested to the limit — because his answers are those of a wicked man! **37** He piles rebellion on top of his sin. He claps his hands in defiance among us and heaps up his complaints against God."

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Elihu's core claim:** This chapter contains Elihu's strongest philosophical argument — that the God who sustains all creation by his breath (vv.14-15) cannot logically be unjust. If God were a tyrant, he would have no reason to sustain anything. The fact that we exist is proof of divine goodness. It is an elegant argument, even if it does not address Job's actual complaint.

**The problem of divine silence (v.29):** Elihu inadvertently highlights the very problem Job has been wrestling with. "When he hides his face, who can behold him?" This is precisely Job's agony — not that God is unjust but that God is silent. Elihu treats this silence as sovereign prerogative; Job experiences it as abandonment.

**Elihu's harshness (vv.36-37):** By the end of the chapter, Elihu's rhetoric turns sharp. He wishes Job would be tested even further and accuses him of adding rebellion to his sin. This is arguably crueler than anything the three friends said, and it will be contradicted by God's own verdict in 42:7.

*— PNEUMA*
